_note: Kept public-safe and template-based, matching codebase-onboarding's eval file: no specific private-repo facts are pre-filled. Point evals 1 and 2 at a repo you have rights to test against and fill in the TEMPLATE fields before running. Eval 3 tests process compliance (how the skill handles a vague scope request) and doesn't require repo-specific facts beyond the substituted repo existing.

evals.name: single-mechanism-template
evals.prompt: Trace exactly how <name a specific mechanism you know well in a repo you have rights to test against, e.g. 'the request-retry logic' or 'the job scheduler'> works, file by file. I need to safely modify it.
evals.expected_output: TEMPLATE — substitute a real, moderately complex mechanism (ideally one with at least one shared state/context object passed between steps, and at least one non-obvious constant/threshold) before running. Write the real expected findings (the actual stage sequence, the actual field names) here so the eval can catch a wrong or incomplete trace, not just a well-formatted one.
expectations: Confirms or restates the subsystem boundary before doing deep research, rather than silently guessing scope from an ambiguous request
Produces a single dense Markdown reference doc, not the 12-item codebase-onboarding report shape
Includes an ordered stage/step table with a file:line citation on every step, not just the ones that were easy to find
If the mechanism passes state between steps via a shared object, includes a field-by-field table naming who writes and who reads each field, cited
Includes a constants/thresholds table for any magic numbers or tunable defaults that control the mechanism's behavior
REPLACE WITH: 1-3 assertions about the exact stage sequence or field names specific to the mechanism you substitute in

evals.name: cleanly-named-subsystem-template
evals.prompt: Deep dive into <a small, cleanly-named subsystem with no real naming ambiguity, in a repo you have rights to test against>.
evals.expected_output: TEMPLATE — substitute a subsystem you've confirmed has no naming traps (no reused identifiers, no misleading names) so this eval specifically checks the skill doesn't manufacture a naming-traps section where none is warranted.
expectations: Does NOT force a 'naming traps' section when the subsystem is genuinely cleanly named — either omits it or states plainly that none were found, rather than inventing a marginal one to fill the section
Scales section count and depth to the subsystem's actual complexity rather than always producing all six possible sections
Every step in the ordered sequence still has a citation despite the doc being short

evals.name: vague-scope-resolution
evals.prompt: Can you deep dive into the caching stuff in this repo?
evals.expected_output: The skill should not silently guess which of possibly several caching-related areas the requester means. It should do a brief orientation pass (grep/glob for the term, or a codebase-memory structural query if available) and state back what it believes the boundary is — e.g. 'I found caching logic in X and Y; I'm scoping this to X, say if you meant Y instead' — before committing to the full deep-dive research effort.
expectations: States back an inferred scope/boundary before or very early in the response, rather than only producing a final report with no scope confirmation at all
The orientation pass is visibly lightweight (a quick search) rather than a full research fan-out used just to resolve scope ambiguity
If the repo substituted for this eval genuinely has only one plausible 'caching' area, the skill may proceed directly — that's also a pass, as long as it names the area it settled on
